title: Trek Stage Planner: Split a Trail into Days
description: Route a trek and split it into stages with distance and climb per day using the Trek Stage Planner — night ends named near real places. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 58-mile trail over five days becomes five stages of about 11–12 miles, each with its climb counted and its ending named — before the boots are bought.
quick_answer: The Trek Stage Planner routes your trail from start to finish, splits it into stages by your number of days or a distance cap per day, and reports each stage's distance and climb with the place it ends near. Build the route, choose the split, review it day by day.
steps_intro: Stages are where a trail becomes a calendar. Cut yours deliberately:

Equal miles are not equal days: the stage with the pass in it deserves to be shorter. Climb per stage is printed precisely so you can un-equalise the split.
Stage ends near places are where beds and shops are argued for. A stage ending nowhere is a camping decision, surfaced early.
The least experienced walker's day is the stage length. Plan stages the whole party can finish smiling.
58 miles ÷ 5 = 11.6 miles a day on average — but the planner shows the split by the route's actual shape, so a river day and a ridge day read differently, as they should.
Set a 15 km daily cap on a 92 km route and the stages count themselves: about six days, each ending where its 15 km ran out.

popular_table.note: Stages split the routed distance; real trails place huts and water where they please, and the planner's named endings are where you negotiate with that reality.

faq: Are the night stops real places with lodging?
The stage ends name the place nearest the split point. Lodging existing there is a booking question — the planner gives you the 'where' to check, early enough to matter.
How are stages split?
By your rule: a fixed day count (distance divided evenly) or a maximum per day (stages accumulate until the cap). Climb is reported per stage so you can adjust.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Trails have weather, daylight and river levels instead of traffic — all yours to read on the day.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Trails wind most of all. Stage distances are the routed ones, the ground your boots will meet.
Can route results change over time?
Paths re-route and bridges wash out; re-plan each season rather than trusting last year's stages.
Can stages be unequal on purpose?
Yes — move a waypoint to where a short day should end and the split re-forms around it. A rest-short day before the pass is craft, not cheating.
Stage times?
Each stage's climb feeds Naismith thinking in the Hiking Route Planner with Elevation — distance stages here, timed stages there.
Stages across a border or a park boundary?
The split is distance-blind to jurisdictions; permits and rules are the planner's human layer on top of the stages.
Can a stage end at a specific hut?
Place a waypoint at the hut and the split bends to it — must-end points are what waypoints are for.
Rest day mid-trek?
Insert it as a zero-distance stage in your calendar; the planner's stages remain the walking days around it.
